A NEW ERA OF ENGAGEMENT

A new framework for designing learning environments where communities build understanding together.

Moving beyond the confines of traditional curriculum. Mosaic empowers learners to investigate authentic, interconnected systems as active agents in a collaborative community of practice.

Explore the Framework Join the Pilot

Why Mosaic?

Traditional schooling divides the world into isolated subjects and treats students as empty vessels to be filled with knowledge. We view learning as an active, social, and systemic journey.

✓
Systems Thinking: Students study real-world connections, not siloed facts.
✓
Student Agency: Learners drive investigations through their own questions and identity.
✓
Community of Practice: The classroom acts as a collaborative research team.

OUR CORE BELIEFS

The Philosophy of Mosaic

We believe learning is a participation-driven process, not a transmission of information.

Shifting the Paradigm

Traditional View

  • Facilitator is the sole source of knowledge
  • Learning is an individual, competitive activity
  • Curriculum is a checklist of isolated standards
  • Success is defined by reproducing answers

Mosaic View

  • Facilitator is the designer of the learning environment
  • Learning is a collaborative, shared process
  • Studios are year-long authentic investigations
  • Success is defined by depth of inquiry and sensemaking
01

Agency Over Compliance

Students are not empty vessels to be filled. They are capable sensemakers who enter the classroom with unique identities, curiosity, and rich prior understandings.

02

Emergence Over Delivery

Knowledge is not transferred; it is constructed. Facilitators do not deliver facts; they design environments where deep understanding can emerge through investigation.

03

Participation Over Silos

Learning is social. Every classroom operates as a Community of Practice where knowledge is built through thinking, questioning, discussing, and reflecting together.

04

Systems Over Subjects

Real-world systems are not divided into subjects. Science, math, engineering, and literacy are deeply interconnected tools used collectively to make sense of complex phenomena.

05

No Facilitator, Yes Facilitation

The facilitator is not the expert standing outside the learning. The facilitator is an expert participant inside the community.

The Studio Facilitator is an expert in designing environments where understanding emerges—not in transferring knowledge.

The Studio Facilitator does not answer questions. The Studio Facilitator helps the community develop better questions.

THE FRAMEWORK

The Studio Framework

A collaborative environment where a community investigates authentic, real-world problems.

How Studios Work

Instead of daily, fragmented lessons, learning is structured around deep, interconnected inquiries called **Studios**. Every Studio starts with a compelling, authentic question that cannot be answered in a single day or by a single subject.

CASE STUDY

"Why is this tree growing differently from the others?"

Click on each node below to see how this single question naturally integrates multiple disciplines without separating them into different subjects.

How does the system work?

Ecosystems

Students investigate the living relationships around the tree. They examine local insects, root symbioses, and nearby plants that might be competing for resources. They ask: *How do these interactions influence the tree's health?*

Weather & Climate

Students look at localized wind patterns, moisture levels, and precipitation history in different spots on campus. They investigate: *Does one area experience micro-climates that stress the tree?*

Sunlight & Energy

Students track the path of the sun, measuring shade cast by buildings or taller trees at different times of the year. They explore the rate of photosynthesis and light absorption.

Soil Chemistry & Biology

Learners take soil samples to test pH levels, moisture retention, organic matter content, and check for the presence of essential soil microbes. They link soil properties directly to plant root absorption.

Force & Gravity

Students study structural mechanics—how physical forces (e.g., wind pushing on the branches, gravity acting on a leaning trunk) affect how the wood grows denser on one side. They learn physics through growth patterns.

Measurement

Learners map the trunk circumference, calculate bark thickness, measure leaf surface area, and track tree height over time. Precision measurements ground their observations in concrete quantitative evidence.

Engineering & Design

Students design physical support systems or soil aeration prototypes to help struggling plants. They model constraints, test materials, and iterate designs based on feedback from the living system.

Mathematics & Data Science

Using the collected data (sunlight hours, soil pH, growth rates), students build scatterplots, calculate means, model growth curves, and run simple statistical correlations to test their hypotheses about the tree.

Practices of a Thinking Community

Our community does not just receive facts. We engage in specific practices to investigate systems and build collaborative understanding. Click a practice card to read its classroom application.

🔍

Notice

Observe carefully before drawing conclusions.

Classroom Context: "I notice the bark is peeling only on the side facing the brick wall."
💡

Wonder

Develop curiosity and meaningful questions.

Classroom Context: "I wonder if the heat radiating from the brick wall at night affects the tree's sleep cycle."
❓

Question

Ask investigable questions that move the community's thinking forward.

Classroom Context: "How does the soil moisture level differ between this tree and the control trees?"
✨

Imagine

Envision possibilities and creative solutions.

Classroom Context: "What if the roots have reached the underground utility line?"
🧩

Decompose

Break complex systems into manageable parts.

Classroom Context: "Let's list the inputs to the tree system: sunlight, water, soil nutrients, air."
📊

Find Patterns

Identify relationships, similarities, differences, and trends.

Classroom Context: "The trees that grow fastest all get shade in the late afternoon."
🎯

Abstract

Focus on what matters most.

Classroom Context: "To model the tree's sun exposure, we can ignore the small branches and treat the canopy as a simple sphere."
🎨

Represent

Express thinking using multiple forms.

Classroom Context: "I drew a diagram showing how carbon cycles through the roots and soil bacteria."
🧪

Investigate

Gather evidence through exploration and testing.

Classroom Context: "Let's pour 1L of water in both areas and measure how long it takes to drain."
🧠

Reason

Use evidence and logic to make sense of ideas.

Classroom Context: "Since the soil tests positive for clay, we know it will hold water longer than sandy soil."
🗣️

Explain

Build and refine explanations.

Classroom Context: "The tree is growing differently because the building blocks sunlight, causing the trunk to lean toward the light source."
⚖️

Argue

Justify ideas using evidence and reasoning.

Classroom Context: "I disagree that it's just sunlight; our soil data shows the pH is 5.5, which is too acidic."
⚙️

Design

Develop and improve solutions.

Classroom Context: "We built a simple rainwater redirector to keep water from pooling around the roots."
🤝

Communicate

Build understanding together.

Classroom Context: "Let's share our findings with the school gardener so they can help monitor it."
🔄

Reflect

Reconsider current understanding and identify new directions.

Classroom Context: "Our initial guess was that bugs were eating the leaves, but now we see it was a nutrient deficiency. What did we miss?"
LEARNING IN ACTION

Active Studios: Grade 3

A year-long journey facilitated by real-world expert missions, not subject divisions.

ACTIVE STUDIO (LONG-YEAR)

Our Living Campus

Instead of separate ecosystems, weather, physics, or geometry units, Grade 3 learners spend the year investigating a single living system on their campus. There are no traditional lesson announcements. Instead, the journey is driven by video messages from real-world facilitators, biologists, engineers, and community stakeholders.

Studio 001: The Launch

Experience how a 45-minute Studio session unfolds. No lectures. No textbook definitions. Only inquiry, systems thinking, and community partner collaboration.

Partner: Apex Parks Dept
Duration: 45 Minutes
Role of Facilitator: Expert Environment Designer (No Knowledge Transfer)

The Video Call

The session begins. The facilitator opens the video stream without warning or intro. The Apex Parks message plays: "We need your help..."

STUDIO FACILITATOR ACTION:

Remains completely silent. No explanation. No introduction to the "Ecosystems Unit". Only silence for 20 seconds as the room processes the request.

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Embrace the Silence.
Do not start with "Today we are learning...". Let the video create the tension. The 20 seconds of silence is crucial to shift the ownership from facilitator-led lecturing to student-led problem-solving.

20
Seconds of Studio Silence

Community Circle

The facilitator gathers the children. Only one question is posed. No judgment, no correction.

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"What stood out to you?"

Responses are limited to neutral prompts: "Tell us more", "Interesting", "What else?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

No Direct Teaching & Multi-Modal Sharing.
Keep inputs neutral. Avoid validating answers. Let students share ideas in whatever way they prefer: some might talk/present, some might draw pictures, and others might sketch graphs or map trends. Support their chosen medium of expression.

Facilitator's Interactive Chalkboard

Click concepts mentioned by students to write them on the board:

Trees Dying Healthy Butterflies Help Park

💡 Note: Children can talk about things not listed here. There is no straight-forward teaching or rigid checklist. Type and add any student concept dynamically.

STUDENT PHRASES RECORDED:
Chalkboard is empty. Click words above to add.

Practice 1: Notice

The facilitator places 10-15 raw photos from the park on the tables. The directive: "Notice as much as you can."

FACILITATOR INQUIRY (DURING TABLE WALK):

"What makes you say that?"

"Is that something you observed, or something you think?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Observation vs. Explanation & Documentation Style.
Separate facts (observations like "exposed roots") from interpretations. Students don't need to write standard paragraphs; they can record evidence by drawing pictures, plotting graphs, or speaking out loud. Honor all forms of record-keeping.

Community Board

Students place observations on the board. The facilitator does not categorize; the community coordinates.

FACILITATOR INTERVENTION:

"Would anyone organize these differently?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Community Coordination & Multi-Modal Stickers.
The Facilitator does not categorize. Let students find patterns. Sticky cards can be drawings, small graphs, text, or equations. Ask "Would anyone organize these differently?" to prompt critical grouping debates.

Practice 2: Wonder

Now, and only now, the questions emerge. No evaluation, no filtering. The wall is covered in wonders.

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"What are you wondering?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Formulate Better Questions.
Shift from seeking answers to formulating questions. Encourage questions starting with "I wonder why..." rather than closed yes/no questions. Questions are the engine of discovery.

The Wonder Wall

Type a wonder question or select one to add to the wall:

Why is this tree leaning? Why is the soil dry here? Do trees share water?
Wonder wall is empty. Post a question.

Practice 3: Build Connections

Students draw lines, connecting questions to see the system. Isolated standards merge into dynamic relationships.

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Systems Thinking.
Prompt students to find relationships between separate facts. Avoid looking at the environment as a list of independent parts. Help them see the feedback loops (e.g. how dry wind accelerates soil evaporation).

System Connections

Click on any two questions to connect them and reveal the system chain:

Why is this tree leaning?
Why is there more wind here?
Why is this soil dry?
Why are there fewer insects?
Select questions to link system relationships.

Practice 4: Community Decision

The community must agree on a focus. The facilitator stays out of the decision.

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"If Apex Parks could answer only ONE of these questions first... which question would help them the most?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Democratic Prioritization.
Let the group debate and decide. Do not interfere with their vote even if you disagree. Agency is built by making real choices and experiencing their research consequences.

The Community Vote
Selected Priority:

Closing Circle

No solutions were reached. Yet, the community has achieved total alignment.

FACILITATOR DIALOGUE:

"Today we didn't solve the problem. What did we accomplish?"

"Tomorrow, we'll decide how to begin investigating."

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

No Final Answers.
Close without a wrap-up lecture. There is no test or graded worksheet. The goal is to leave the studio with a shared system map and high motivation to investigate the chosen thread in the next session.

Studio Reflection Summary
  • Noticing: 15 detailed environmental observations recorded.
  • Wondering: 8 systemic questions generated.
  • Connecting: Relationships mapped between soil depth, wind load, and ecosystem health.

Closing the Loop

Instead of writing a homework assignment for a facilitator, groups submit their findings back to the community partner. This is real.

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Authentic Feedback Loop & Flexible Output.
Connect research to the real-world partner. The final report doesn't need to be text-only; support students in submitting hand-drawn maps, graphs of variables, slides, or audio explanations. Build agency through output choice.

Studio 002: A New Message Has Arrived

Explore the second day of Grade 3. Students synthesize yesterday's feedback, analyze 8 new detail photos, discover ecosystem patterns, separate signal from noise, and prep for their first campus observation field trip.

Partner: Apex Parks Dept
Duration: 45 Minutes
Role of Facilitator: Environment Facilitator (Prompting Systemic Analysis)

A New Message

The session begins. The facilitator opens the video update from Ranger Marcus immediately. Children realize the community partner is listening: "Thank you for your first report. We were surprised..."

STUDIO FACILITATOR ACTION:

Remains completely silent. No initial lecturing. Let the feedback from the partner speak for itself and build student ownership.

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Connecting Across Sessions.
Show students that their work has an immediate, real-world impact. The partner's video call is a direct reaction to Report 1, establishing that their research is not a simulation, but an active collaboration.

"Good morning, Studio Team. Thank you for your first report. We were surprised by your observations. Many of you noticed the soil. Many of you wondered about the wind. Our park ranger collected a little more information for you yesterday. We hope it helps."

Deeper Reflection

The facilitator displays yesterday's community report. Students are asked to reflect and see if they want to add anything after watching today's message.

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"Does anyone want to add something after watching today's message?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Build on Community Capital.
Do not start fresh as if yesterday didn't happen. Help students connect the thread. Support multiple modes of sharing (e.g. students can present verbally, draw extra notes, or sketch simple diagrams of new ideas).

Observe & Connect

The facilitator introduces 8 new detail photos from Ranger Marcus. Students analyze them to connect old observations with new ecosystem variables (puddles, shade, cracks, healthy straight trees).

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"What new details do these photos reveal about our soil and trees?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

UDL Documentation.
Children don't need to write text logs. They can zoom into photos (click to zoom) to see details, sketch patterns, or compare straight vs. leaning trunks. Let them document evidence in drawings or spoken notes.

Find Patterns

Students begin finding recurring relationships. No formulas or lectures: just mapping cause-and-effect lines across factors.

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"What patterns are beginning to appear?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Systems Thinking Patterning.
Do not teach "Ecosystem Interactions" as a definition. Let students discover them by building cause-and-effect paths. Accept different, plausible models from groups without imposing a single correct link.

Ecosystem Pattern Builder

Click variables in order to establish a chain pattern of relationship:

Build a pattern chain (e.g. Healthy Trees âž” More Shade...)

Data Abstraction

Students learn to filter out the noise. They separate minor details from the primary ecological signals that explain the problem.

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"Out of everything we noticed... which observations might actually help explain our problem?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Information Synthesis.
Help students filter out noise. Drawing a graph or cataloging minor facts (e.g., number of leaves) is less helpful than focusing on systemic patterns (e.g. slope wind, drying topsoil).

Observation Signal Filter

Classify each observation as either a Key Signal or Background Noise:

"One oak tree has 12 leaves on a lower branch."
"Soil is much drier in wind-exposed zones."
"One exposed root is exactly 4.2 centimeters thick."
"Leaning tree trunks all face away from the windward slope."
"A small green plastic bottle is near the park walkway."
"Soil is darker and wetter under the healthy tree canopy."

Investigation Planning

Students do not build a lab experiment yet. Instead, they plan variables for tomorrow's field visit: "If we went to the park tomorrow, what would we need to look at?"

FACILITATOR INQUIRY:

"If we went to the park tomorrow... what would we need to look at?"

FACILITATOR FOCUS:

Goal Alignment.
Let them structure their own investigation variables. Do not hand out a pre-printed lab template. By aligning parameters now, they build agency and ownership over tomorrow's observations.

EMPIRICAL FOUNDATIONS

Research & Foundations

Built on verified educational theories of learning, identity, and complex systems.

Communities of Practice (Lave & Wenger)

Learning is not an individual cognitive state, but an interactive process of participation within a community. Mosaic shifts classrooms from spaces of solitary listening to communities of practice where students work as active researchers.

Systems Thinking in Education

Understanding real-world problems requires understanding loops, connections, structures, and behaviors over time. By teaching with year-long integrated missions rather than isolated weekly topics, students build complex cognitive schemata of interconnected systems.

Sensemaking and Identity (Lave, Wenger, Nasir)

When students work on authentic problems that impact their local spaces (like their school campus or neighborhood), they develop a sense of identity as mathematical, scientific, and design thinkers. They see that they belong in STEAM fields because their identity and agency are centered.

WHO WE ARE

The Mosaic Movement

A collective of educators, designers, and researchers rewriting the framework of learning.

Mosaic was founded on a simple realization: **the educational system is designed for a world that no longer exists.**

When we divide knowledge into separate subjects, we teach children that the world is made of isolated parts. But our world's greatest challenges—climate change, energy, public health, structural inequality—are interconnected systems.

Mosaic provides a new framework for designing learning environments where communities build understanding together. By centering student identity, protecting natural curiosity, and fostering a collaborative Community of Practice, we prepare learners to think, collaborate, and design in a complex world.

"We do not teach subjects. We coordinate the community's sensemaking of the world."
— The Mosaic Design Group
